The absence of a representative benchmark has thus far hindered comparison with traditional agricultural techniques. This paper aims to establish the current status and future prospects of energy efficiency in vertical farming by exploring the interplay between plant physiology and facility design and operation. Energy use is primarily driven by the need to control the physical environment for crop productivity and quality, resulting in specific lighting and climate control requirements. While artificial lighting technologies are advancing towards the current biological limits of photosynthesis, climate control is increasingly influenced by plant physiological activity. An analysis of studies focusing on energy use in vertical farming reveals a current specific energy consumption of 10–18 kWh kg−1 for lettuce production, corresponding to an energy use intensity of 850–1150 kWh m−2 year−1. Consideration of theoretical crop energy requirements, together with expected advances in equipment efficiency and operational control strategies, suggests a technical energy benchmark of 3.1–7.4 kWh kg−1. Despite projected gains in energy efficiency, the current economic costs and environmental impacts associated with increased electricity use highlight significant challenges to the short-term energy sustainability of vertical farming.

Historical baseline data from industry surveys indicate a broad average consumption of 38.8\text{ kWh kg}^{-1} for fresh leafy greens grown in commercial vertical farms [cite: 6]. High-performing, modern operational facilities achieve benchmarks between 10\text{ and }18\text{ kWh kg}^{-1} [cite: 6, 13], while standard grid-powered vertical systems frequently operate within 10\text{ to }12.5\text{ kWh kg}^{-1} [cite: 7].

Indeed, recent estimates show that it takes between 10 and 18 kilowatt-hours to grow one kilogram of lettuce in a stacked system—a figure that dwarfs the less-than-1 kilowatt-hour needed for traditional field production. Such a gulf makes it clear that any sustainable future for controlled-environment agriculture hinges on smarter lighting, sharper climate controls, and a reliable mix of renewable power. Even so, key knowledge gaps persist. Most urgently, the field still lacks large-scale, real-world data and agreed-upon benchmarks to judge whether specific energy-saving measures really work. Many current studies overlook the practical integration of renewable energy and rarely address solutions accessible to small-scale operators. Additionally, workforce training and public acceptance are underexplored, ultimately constraining the real-world sustainability and scalability of vertical farming systems.

VFs' capacities to achieve close-to potential yields and to drastically reduce environmental impacts are topics of current discourse, but comparable supporting data is limited. We present the first quantitative review of case studies on environmental life cycle assessments (LCAs) of lettuce-producing VFs. After deriving farm-based key performance indicators (KPIs), we remodeled the LCAs with harmonized system boundaries and electricity datasets under current and future energy scenarios, and provided suggestions for better KPI reporting and achieving more comprehensive VF-LCAs. The case studies' annual productivity ranged from 7–97 kg m − 2 cultivation area (median: 62 kg m − 2 ), while energy use efficiency ranged from 10–39 kWh kg − 1 (median: 18 kWh kg − 1 ), and irrigation water use efficiency from 1.4–52 L kg − 1 (median: 15 L kg − 1 ). Wide ranges of KPIs can be explained by gaps in data reporting and unclear terminology, differences in VF typologies, lettuce cultivar choice, and yield-optimizing management strategies. Harmonizing and remodeling the LCAs confirmed on-farm energy use and choice of energy sources as main drivers of greenhouse gas emissions. The case studies reported emissions of 0.18–32 kg CO 2eq kg − 1 without their electricity datasets being harmonized, whereas harmonizing them on Dutch grid electricity resulted in 4.8–16 kg CO 2eq kg − 1 (median: 7.6 kg CO 2eq kg − 1 ). Our projections based on decarbonized electricity grids of 2050 showed that most environmental impacts can be reduced by ~ 30–70% relative to 2020.

VF has a much lower land and water footprint compared to conventional agriculture, but its energy footprint—particularly for LED lighting, HVAC and pumping can be considerable. Preliminary life cycle assessments indicate energy consumption of 5–10 kWh per kg of lettuce grown in VF systems, compared to 0.2–0.5 kWh per kg for lettuce grown in the field [ 198 ]. Vertical farming bankruptcies happen when indoor farming companies cannot generate enough revenue to cover their operating costs, which are dominated by energy (lighting and climate control), labor, and debt service on massive upfront capital investments. The core problem is structural: vertical farms replace free sunlight and rain with electricity and engineered systems, and the resulting produce often can't command enough of a price premium to cover the difference. According to iGrow News, the 2025 bankruptcy wave included “silent bankruptcies” — companies that quietly exited or were acquired before formally filing, meaning the actual financial stress across the sector is worse than the public numbers suggest.

However, this structural transition introduces a fundamental thermodynamic paradox. Open-field farming relies on free solar radiation and natural precipitation, incurring operational costs primarily through land, diesel, fertilizer, labor, and localized irrigation. In contrast, vertical farming substitutes free natural inputs with capital-intensive building infrastructure, engineering controls, and continuously billed electrical power [cite: 4, 6, 7]. The agricultural footprint is compressed horizontally by stacking production layers, but this spatial compression comes at the cost of high energy requirements per kilogram of marketable produce [cite: 4, 6, 7].

Abstract Vertical farming is a relatively new fresh fruit and vegetable production system, where lamps (mostly light emitting diodes [LED]) are the sole light source. A high light use efficiency (LUEinc), defined as shoot dry weight per incident photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD; g mol−1) integral, is crucial for the economic viability of vertical farming. Very different values for LUEinc have been reported in the literature and it is not clear whether LUEinc is higher in vertical farming than in greenhouse or open field cultivation. Values of LUEinc of lettuce grown in a vertical farm (53 studies), greenhouse (13 studies) and open field (8 studies) were collected from literature, as well as relevant cultivation aspects such as lettuce weight at harvest, cultivation period (plant age at harvest), daily light integral, cumulative daily light integral for the whole cultivation period, planting density and CO2 concentration. The average LUEinc for lettuce grown in a vertical farm was 0.55 g mol−1 which was higher than 0.39 g mol−1 for greenhouse- grown lettuce. Both were substantially higher than for field- grown lettuce (0.23 g mol−1). The maximum measured LUEinc for lettuce grown in a vertical farm (1.63 g mol−1) is close to the published maximum theoretical value, which ranges from 1.26 to 1.81 g mol−1. Since all environmental factors can be fully controlled, vertical farming has the capability to achieve the theoretical maximum LUEinc. Using the highest reported LUEinc based on shoot fresh weight (44 g mol−1 at 200 μmol m−2 s−1 PPFD and 16 h photoperiod), it is estimated that each layer of a vertical farm can potentially produce annually up to 700 kg of lettuce per m2 at 500 μmol m−2 s−1 of continuous light.

Based on Carotti et al.  (2021) who observed an incident LUEinc in fresh weight of 44 g mol−1 (as observed in plants grown at 200 μmol m−2 s−1 PPFD and 16 h photoperiod), potential annual lettuce production was estimated for several combinations of photoperiod and incident PPFD (Figure 2). Since the lettuce cultivated in a vertical farm is clean, total shoot weight is taken as harvestable weight. Potential annual yield was only 35 kg m−2 year−1 when grown at 50 μmol m−2  s−1 and a photoperiod of 12 h but reached up to 700 kg m−2 year−1 when grown at 500 μmol m−2 s−1 and a photoperiod of 24 h.

However, maintaining these yields requires substantial power inputs per square meter of facility footprint [cite: 13, 14]. 6.1. AeroFarms—Data-Driven Aeroponic Vertical Farming (USA)One of the first commercial scale aeroponic VF operators, AeroFarms was founded in Newark, New Jersey in 2004. The company uses a proprietary aeroponic system, combined with thousands of sensors and ML models that create crop-specific recipes for growth [ 175 ]. Their flagship Newark facility opened in 2016 and is 69,000 sq ft, billed as the world’s largest VF, followed by an R&D-focused site in Danville, Virginia and a 95,000 sq ft production farm in Compton, California [ 22 , 54 ]. AeroFarms produces over 300 varieties of leafy greens, microgreens, herbs, and salad mixes, with a yield 390 times greater per square foot than traditional field agriculture, in as little as 16–20 days [ 75 ]. The sustainability claims include 95% water reduction, zero pesticide use and significantly reduced land footprint [ 35 , 63 , 172 , 176 ]. Location near major urban markets means less transport, less food miles and less spoilage. AeroFarms has been a Certified B Corporation for many years, a testament to its commitment to environmental and social governance standards. Critical Assessment: AeroFarms showed its technical sophistication and operational capability but filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023 and restructured in 2024, exposing the financial fragility of the pure-play VF model despite technological leadership [ 175 , 176 ]. Aeroponic systems are still a large contributor to operational costs in terms of energy intensity, especially LED lighting and high-pressure misting. Independent verification of yield and resource efficiency claims is limited, and the bulk of data comes from company reports, not third-party audits. The long-term economic viability of the aeroponic model at scale is not yet proven.

6.3. Gotham Greens—Controlled Environment Greenhouse–Vertical Hybrids (USA)Founded in Brooklyn in 2009, Gotham Greens uses a hybrid model of recirculating hydroponics (mostly NFT) in high-tech greenhouses with climate control and supplemental LED lighting [ 177 , 178 ]. The company opened the first commercial-scale rooftop hydroponic farm in NYC (Greenpoint, 15,000 sq ft) and has now expanded to a network of large greenhouses in multiple states. As of 2024, Gotham Greens has 13 greenhouses with about 2 million sq ft of growing space, with facilities ranging in size from 200,000 to 540,000 sq ft in Virginia, Texas and Georgia. Key crops are leafy greens, herbs and salad kits, with recent expansion into value-added products such as dressings and dips. Reportedly the yield per acre is 20–30 times higher than produce grown in the field. Water reduction is 95%, land reduction is 97%, pesticides are zero, and renewable energy is used in most facilities [ 179 ]. Proximity to large cities means shorter supply chains that lower emissions and fresher products. Critical Assessment: The hybrid greenhouse–VF approach uses natural sunlight and therefore has about 30–40% lower energy costs compared to pure indoor vertical farms that rely completely on artificial lighting. This hybrid model probably offers more resilience and lower operational risk. But geographic expansion is limited by regional insolation patterns, and the model is still reliant on access to appropriate greenhouse locations near urban markets. The hybrid approach may not be as technologically ambitious as pure indoor farms, but it may offer a more sustainable economic pathway.

6.5. Plenty—Large-Scale AI and Robotics Vertical Farming (USA)Plenty, founded in San Francisco in 2014, is among the most heavily funded VF companies globally, having raised some USD 1 billion and achieving a peak valuation of over USD 1.4 billion [ 32 , 180 ]. The company’s technology platform includes tall vertical towers (up to 30 feet high) densely packed with plants, full-spectrum LEDs, robotics for harvesting, and extensive sensor networks feeding AI/ML models for environmental optimization. Plenty began with leafy greens but shifted to berries, especially strawberries, in a partnership with Driscoll’s, the world’s biggest berry marketer [ 180 ]. Key facilities are a former leafy greens farm in Compton, California, that was repurposed; Richmond, Virginia, the company’s first vertical strawberry farm; Laramie, Wyoming, an R&D center; and an international site in Abu Dhabi. The company grows leafy greens, strawberries and tomatoes and has tested more than 50 crops. Reported yields are between 150 and 350× per acre over conventional farming, with 90–95% water reduction and zero pesticide use [ 35 , 181 ]. Critical Assessment Plenty’s decision to close the Compton facility and refocus on berries was considered by industry observers to be a setback, demonstrating that leafy-green economics remain difficult even for well-capitalized operations [ 35 , 181 ]. Energy use per kg of produce is still above field production and long-term profitably will depend on premium pricing for berries and continued cost reduction in LED and automation technologies. The company’s overseas expansion adds to the operational and logistical complexity. The model is technically ambitious, but its economic sustainability at scale remains to be demonstrated.

3.2.1. Hydroponics: The Pillar of Vertical FarmingHydroponics is the most widely used technique in vertical farming. Plants grow in nutrient-enriched water solutions, with roots supported by inert media such as perlite, rockwool, or coconut coir [ 77 , 78 ]. Common setups include the Nutrient Film Technique (NFT) and Deep Water Culture (DWC) This method excels with leafy greens, herbs, and strawberries, often delivering yields up to 11 times higher than conventional field production for crops, such as lettuce [ 79 , 80 , 81 ]. Its strengths are clear: water use can be reduced by approximately 70% through recirculation, sometimes supplemented with graywater or rainwater. The soilless system minimizes soil-borne diseases and supports clean and high-quality output. These characteristics make hydroponics particularly attractive in urban environments. By 2024, it accounted for 47–65% of the VF market share, largely due to its relatively accessible setup costs and operational simplicity [ 6 , 82 , 83 , 84 ]. However, challenges remain. Upfront investment in equipment and lighting is considerable, and energy consumption can be substantially higher than that of traditional farming. Waterborne pathogens can spread rapidly without vigilant monitoring. Fortunately, advances in IoT controls and renewable energy integration are gradually alleviating these constraints [ 85 ]. Overall, hydroponics continues to serve as a reliable foundation for most commercial VF operations [ 79 , 86 , 87 , 88 , 89 , 90 ]. Advancements in renewable energy and IoT-based systems have effectively counterbalanced hydroponics’ disadvantages. Hydroponics remains at the core of VF, providing ease of access and high yields [ 6 , 39 , 84 , 91 ].

This study assessed whether different combinations of photoperiod and photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD; 16 L:8 D at 250 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, 12 L:12 D at 340 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, and continuous 24 L:0 D at 170 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹) affect growth, physiology, and energy performance of two crisphead lettuce cultivars [( Lactuca sativa L. var. crispa - 'Falstaff' (green) and 'Copacabana' (red)] when the daily light integral (DLI) is maintained constant (14.4 mol m⁻² day⁻¹). Yield, morphological traits, chlorophyll fluorescence, and gas exchange parameters did not differ among lighting treatments, indicating comparable photosynthetic functioning under all photoperiod–PPFD combinations. However, continuous lighting (24 L:0 D) improved energy use efficiency (EUE) and light use efficiency (LUE), while reducing lighting costs per unit of produced biomass and demonstrating a clear benefit in terms of resource utilization. Cultivar-related differences were more pronounced than treatment effects, with red lettuce showing higher levels of phenolic compounds, carotenoids, anthocyanins, and antioxidant capacity, while maintaining similar morphological responses. Overall, the results show that under a constant DLI, photoperiod manipulation obtained by adjusting PPFD has a limited impact on plant physiology but can substantially influence yield and energy efficiency. Continuous moderate-intensity lighting thus emerges as an effective strategy to enhance the economic and environmental sustainability of VFs without compromising crop performance.

Operational research demonstrates that photoperiod manipulation and spectral tuning can significantly improve Light Use Efficiency (LUE) and Energy Use Efficiency (EUE) without compromising physiological development [cite: 15, 16]. Maintaining a constant Daily Light Integral (DLI) of 14.4\text{ mol m}^{-2}\text{day}^{-1} while shifting from a standard photoperiod (16\text{ hours light : } 8\text{ hours dark} at 250 \mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1} photosynthetic photon flux density [PPFD]) to a continuous lighting regime (24\text{ hours light : } 0\text{ hours dark} at 170 \mu\text{mol m}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1} PPFD) yields equivalent fresh weight and physiological performance [cite: 15]. Crucially, continuous low-intensity lighting increases EUE and LUE, lowers peak thermal loading, reduces required HVAC cooling capacity, and lowers capital equipment costs [cite: 15].

Continuous light (24 L:0 D) has kept stable lettuce yield ( Table 2) and reduced LED electricity costs, thereby improving energy use efficiency (EUE) and light use efficiency (LUE) compared with 12 L:12 D and 16 L:8 D photoperiods ( Table 4). These improvements derive from distributing the same DLI over a longer photoperiod, which reduces instantaneous power demand and enhances lighting efficiency, as previously reported for VFs ( Graamans et al., 2018 ; Stanghellini and Katzin, 2024 ). Nevertheless, artificial lighting remained the dominant energy cost, in line with reports indicating that lighting typically accounts for 60–85% of total energy consumption in indoor farming systems ( Yorifuji and Obara, 2022 ).

Why did AeroFarms go bankrupt?AeroFarms filed for Chapter 11 in June 2023, citing capital market headwinds. It emerged from bankruptcy in September 2023 and refinanced in August 2025, but its largest investor withdrew funding in December 2025, forcing permanent closure of its Virginia facility and laying off 173 workers. The core issue was inability to generate enough revenue from produce sales to cover the massive operating costs of its facilities.Can vertical farms ever be profitable?Some already are, but typically at smaller scales, in specific geographies with cheap energy or high produce prices, and growing high-value crops. The path to profitability requires proven unit economics before scaling, patient capital, location-specific advantages, and increasingly, automation to reduce labor costs. The VC model of “scale fast, figure out profitability later” has been the primary failure mode.

Strategic Industry Outlook and Actionable ConclusionsThe structural correction of the controlled environment agriculture sector highlights several core economic lessons:Energy-Location Coupling is Mandatory: Vertical farming cannot function as a geography-agnostic commercial real estate model. Long-term viability requires co-locating facilities directly with low-cost renewable energy, waste-heat capture infrastructure, or microgrid connections that can secure off-peak power rates below \$0.03\text{--}\$0.05\text{ per kWh} [cite: 1, 6, 7]. Operating on standard urban industrial retail power tariffs (\$0.10\text{--}\$0.20+\text{ per kWh}) creates a recurring cost structure that cannot compete with open-field or greenhouse production [cite: 6, 7].Dynamic Photobiology Optimizes HVAC CapEx: Photoperiod flattening (24\text{L}:0\text{D} photoperiods) and dynamic red-blue spectral adjustment reduce peak electrical draw, lower necessary HVAC cooling tonnages, and improve energy use efficiency (EUE) [cite: 15, 16]. These operational strategies lower initial equipment CapEx while reducing lighting electricity expenses by up to 40% [cite: 15, 16].CapEx Rationalization Over Excessive Automation: Over-automating material handling via custom robotics adds significant upfront debt and ongoing depreciation expenses that often outweigh direct labor savings [cite: 23, 26]. Successful operators favor modular designs with targeted automation limited to repetitive tasks like seeding, transplanting, and harvesting [cite: 23, 26].Crop Selection Beyond the "Lettuce Trap": Selling commodity leafy greens at standard retail prices exposes vertical farms to compressed gross margins [cite: 6, 12]. Long-term commercial viability requires prioritizing crops with high value per unit of fresh biomass—such as culinary herbs, specialized pharmaceutical inputs, high-density propagation seedlings, gourmet mushrooms, and specialty berries [cite: 6, 8, 11, 22].
